sheet.howExamined: B2, 1 hour 15 minutes: 70 marks at Foundation, 80 at Higher, calculator allowed. Disease tends to come early as a matching exercise or a table worth three to five marks, pairing each disease with its pathogen, its route, or how it is prevented and treated (Summer 2022 Foundation Q1 and Higher Q3, Summer 2023 Foundation Q1), followed by single-mark recall such as the drug that treats a bacterial infection. Aseptic technique turns up on both papers but mostly in Unit 7 Booklet B: an apparatus name [1], the barely lifted lid [1], the 25 °C limit with its reason [1], and a six-mark banded description of the whole transfer (Summer 2024).
traps: Filing a sexually transmitted infection under the wrong pathogen, a bacterial one for a viral one or the reverse (Summer 2025 B2 Foundation Q6 and Higher Q2)
Writing antibodies for the drug that treats a bacterial infection, and not knowing the word aseptic for the set of techniques (Summer 2023 B2 Foundation Q1)

Listing the Bunsen burner among the things an autoclave sterilises, and muddling what the half-closed lid is for: it keeps microorganisms carried in the air from getting onto the agar, not air itself and not bacteria leaving (Summer 2023 Unit 7 Biology Booklet B Higher Q3)
Not knowing the name inoculating loop, and taking bacteria from the bottle before flaming the loop, which kills the culture (Summer 2024 Unit 7 Biology Booklet B, Q2 at Higher and Q4 at Foundation)
Explaining why benches are cleaned by saying bacteria cause disease, instead of saying the cleaning kills or removes them (Summer 2024 Unit 7 Biology Booklet B Q2)
Missing 25 °C, or giving it without the reason, which is avoiding the growth of pathogens (Summer 2025 Unit 7 Biology Booklet B Higher Q3)
Treating flu or HIV with antibiotics: antibiotics only kill bacteria
Dividing by every guest instead of by the people who ate that food, when working out a percentage from outbreak data

noteBlocks.lede: Some diseases can be caught and some cannot. This topic is about the ones that can: the bacteria, viruses and fungi behind them, how each one travels and is stopped, and how scientists grow bacteria safely without letting anything else in.
can: Name the pathogen behind each of the eight diseases CCEA lists, and say how each one spreads.
Say how each disease is prevented and treated, and why antibiotics never treat a virus.
Describe aseptic technique step by step, with the reason for every step.

noteBlocks.text: Health, communicable diseases and aseptic technique

noteBlocks.md: In 1845 a fungus reached Ireland's potato fields. Within weeks the leaves blackened and the potatoes rotted in the ground, and about a million people died in the famine that followed. Potato blight is one of eight diseases on your specification, and every one of them is caused by a pathogen too small to see.

Viruses: a six-sided protein coat with spikes and genetic material inside; HIV leading to AIDS, cold and flu, and HPV. Fungi: threads with round spore cases releasing spores; athlete's foot and potato blight.

noteBlocks.md:
**Health**, in CCEA's words, is being free from **communicable** and **non-communicable** disease.

A communicable disease is caused by a **pathogen** (a bacterium, a virus or a fungus) and can pass from person to person. A non-communicable disease has no pathogen, so it cannot be caught.

noteBlocks.alt: A diagram: health means being free from both kinds of disease. Communicable diseases are caused by a pathogen and can pass from person to person, for example flu, tuberculosis and HPV. Non-communicable diseases have no pathogen and cannot be caught, for example lung cancer and Type 2 diabetes.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of these is a communicable disease?
noteBlocks.explain: Tuberculosis. It is caused by a bacterium and spreads in droplets when someone coughs. Lung cancer and Type 2 diabetes have no pathogen, so nobody can catch them.

noteBlocks.md:
**Bacteria** are living cells, much smaller than yours, with no nucleus. **Viruses** are smaller still and are not cells at all: a virus can only reproduce inside one of your cells, damaging it as it does. **Fungi** grow as threads and release **spores**.

CCEA names eight diseases, and the marks go to knowing which group each one belongs to. **Bacteria:** chlamydia, salmonella, tuberculosis. **Viruses:** HIV (which leads to AIDS), cold and flu, HPV. **Fungi:** athlete's foot, potato blight.

noteBlocks.why: A second explanation of communicable and non-communicable disease. It is made for another exam board, so if it names a disease that is not one of CCEA's eight, let that one pass.

noteBlocks.explain: A virus. HPV is easy to misfile because it can lead to cancer, but its pathogen is a virus, and a vaccine is how it is prevented.

noteBlocks.alt: Four routes of spread. Droplets in the air from coughs and sneezes carry tuberculosis, colds and flu. Food and drink, such as undercooked chicken or eggs, or food handled with dirty hands, carry salmonella. Sex and body fluids carry chlamydia, HIV and HPV, and HIV also passes through shared needles. Touch and spores carry athlete's foot, from damp floors and towels, and potato blight, whose spores travel on wind and rain.

noteBlocks.md: Prevention blocks the route: condoms, thorough cooking and hand washing, **vaccination** against tuberculosis, flu and HPV, fungicide on potato crops. Treatment depends on the pathogen: **antibiotics** kill bacteria, antiviral drugs slow HIV but cannot cure it, and antifungal cream clears athlete's foot.

noteBlocks.title: Why an antibiotic never cures flu
noteBlocks.md: An antibiotic attacks parts that only bacteria have. A virus has none of them, and it reproduces inside your own cells, so the antibiotic has nothing to act on. Flu is treated with rest and fluids while your body's defences clear it.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of these diseases could a doctor treat with antibiotics?
noteBlocks.explain: Chlamydia, because it is caused by a bacterium. Flu and HIV are viruses, and antibiotics do nothing to them.

noteBlocks.md: To study bacteria, scientists grow them on **agar**, a nutrient jelly in a Petri dish, or in nutrient broth. **Aseptic technique** keeps other microorganisms out of the culture, and the culture off you. First **sterilise**: autoclave the Petri dishes, culture media and culture bottles, heat the **inoculating loop** in a Bunsen flame until it glows red, and wipe the bench with alcohol. Work beside the flame, and lift the dish's lid only a little.

noteBlocks.prompt: When bacteria are streaked onto agar, why is the Petri dish lid lifted only a little?
options: to stop microorganisms from the air landing on the agar
to stop the bacteria escaping from the dish
noteBlocks.answer: to stop microorganisms from the air landing on the agar
noteBlocks.explain: The danger drifts in from the air. A barely lifted lid lets the loop in while it shields the agar underneath.

noteBlocks.text: 8. Seal it, incubate it, get rid of it

noteBlocks.alt: A Petri dish of pale agar seen from above. Dense orange streaks of bacteria run down the left side, thinning towards the right into separate round orange colonies; a small paper label is stuck on the agar near the bottom.
noteBlocks.credit: Rosanna Hartline (RosieScienceGal), Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
noteBlocks.caption: A real streak plate after incubation. Every colony is the same kind, and every one grew where the loop went.
noteBlocks.prompt: Every colony here looks alike. What would a contaminated plate look like, and which step of aseptic technique stops that happening?

noteBlocks.md: After streaking, **tape the lid on** and label the dish. Incubate it at a **maximum of 25 °C**. Bacteria that cause disease in humans grow best near body temperature, 37 °C, so keeping well below that avoids growing a **pathogen** by accident. When you have finished, **autoclave** the cultures to kill them before they are thrown away, then clean the bench and wash your hands.

noteBlocks.title: 25 °C and its reason
noteBlocks.md: On the Summer 2025 Unit 7 Biology practical paper, most candidates could name the Bunsen burner, but fewer could give 25 °C. The number and its reason travel together: 25 °C, to avoid growing pathogens.

noteBlocks.prompt: What is the maximum temperature, in °C, at which bacterial cultures should be incubated in a school laboratory?
noteBlocks.explain: 25 °C. Anything warmer, and especially 37 °C, risks growing bacteria that cause disease in people.

steps.working: (b) A hot loop would kill the bacteria it is meant to transfer.
steps.decision: Sterilising the loop and keeping the culture alive are both the point, so the order is heat, cool, then touch.

options: Because heat kills the bacteria in the culture as well
Because a hot loop melts the plastic dish
Because the loop is only sterile once it is cold
whyMenu.explain: Heat does not choose. Whatever kills unwanted microorganisms on the loop kills the culture too.

steps.working: (c) To avoid growing pathogens: bacteria that cause disease in humans are adapted to body temperature, 37 °C, so at 25 °C or below they are unlikely to grow.

items.stem: Before we start, three things you have met before. Which structure does a bacterial cell NOT have?

options.feedback: A nucleus. Its DNA lies loose in the cytoplasm, which is why a bacterium is drawn with a loop of DNA.
Bacteria do have a membrane, just inside their cell wall. What they lack is a nucleus.
Every cell has cytoplasm. The missing structure is the nucleus.
Bacteria have a cell wall, though not one made of cellulose. What they lack is a nucleus.

items.stem: What does the word 'sterile' mean when it describes a dish or a tool?

options.text: It has no living microorganisms on it
options.feedback: Nothing alive on it: no bacteria, no fungal spores. Aseptic technique is built on this idea.
A dish can look spotless and still carry thousands of bacteria. Sterile means nothing alive at all.

options.text: It has been washed in cold water
options.feedback: Cold water removes dirt but leaves microorganisms alive.
Sterile is about living things, not chemicals.

items.stem: Why does food keep for longer in a fridge?
items.skill: Link temperature to the growth of microorganisms

options.text: The cold slows the growth of bacteria
options.feedback: Cold slows bacteria right down. The same idea, run the other way, explains why incubators are kept below body temperature.

options.text: The cold kills all the bacteria
options.feedback: Most bacteria survive in a fridge; they just grow very slowly. That is why chilled food still has a use-by date.
A fridge is full of air. It works by keeping the food cold.

options.text: Bacteria cannot live in the dark
options.feedback: Darkness does not stop bacteria. The low temperature slows them.

items.stem: HPV is caused by which type of microorganism?
items.skill: Name the pathogen type for a CCEA disease

options.feedback: A virus. HPV can lead to cervical cancer, and a vaccine is how it is prevented.
The three bacterial diseases are chlamydia, salmonella and tuberculosis. HPV is viral.
The fungal diseases are athlete's foot and potato blight. HPV is viral.

items.stem: Which of these diseases could be treated with antibiotics?

options.feedback: Chlamydia is bacterial, so antibiotics treat it.
Flu is caused by a virus, and antibiotics only kill bacteria. Rest and fluids are the treatment.
HIV is a virus. Antiviral drugs slow it, but antibiotics do nothing to it.
Athlete's foot is a fungus, treated with antifungal cream.

items.stem: Which is CCEA's definition of health?

options.text: Being free from communicable and non-communicable disease
options.feedback: The specification's own words. Learn it as written.
A strong immune system helps, but the definition is about being free from disease.

options.text: Never having caught a communicable disease
options.feedback: Half of it: health also means being free from non-communicable disease.

options.text: Being able to exercise without getting tired
options.feedback: That describes fitness, not health as CCEA defines it.

items.stem: Which of these is sterilised in an autoclave before bacteria are grown?

options.text: the Petri dishes and culture media
options.feedback: Everything the culture will touch goes into the autoclave: dishes, media, bottles.
The Bunsen burner is the tool that sterilises the loop. It is never autoclaved.
The bench is wiped with alcohol or disinfectant; it cannot go into an autoclave.
Hands are washed. An autoclave uses steam under high pressure.

items.stem: During inoculation, a Petri dish is opened only a crack. Why?
items.skill: Explain a step of aseptic technique

options.text: To stop microorganisms from the air landing on the agar
options.feedback: The danger drifts in from the air. A barely lifted lid lets the loop in and little else.

options.text: To stop the bacteria escaping into the room
options.feedback: The lid is shut and taped afterwards for that. During inoculation the risk is things getting in.

options.text: To keep the air out so the bacteria cannot respire
options.feedback: Air itself is not the problem; the microorganisms carried in it are.
Temperature is set in the incubator. The lid keeps out microorganisms from the air.

items.stem: Why are cultures in a school laboratory incubated at no more than 25 °C?

options.text: To avoid growing bacteria that cause disease in humans
options.feedback: Pathogens grow best near body temperature. Staying well below it keeps them from growing.

options.text: So the bacteria grow as fast as possible
options.feedback: The limit is about safety, not speed. Warmer would be faster, and that is the danger.
Many bacteria grow very well above 25 °C, including the ones that make people ill.
Agar stays solid far above body temperature. The limit is about pathogens.

items.stem: What is the tool called that carries bacteria from a culture onto an agar plate?

options.feedback: An inoculating loop: a wire with a small ring at its tip. Both words are expected.
A pipette moves measured volumes of liquid. The streaking tool is an inoculating loop.
Forceps pick things up. The tool that transfers bacteria is an inoculating loop.
A spatula moves powders. Bacteria are transferred with an inoculating loop.

parts.stem: The diagram shows apparatus used to transfer bacteria from a culture bottle onto an agar plate. Label A, B, C and D, choosing names from the list.

scheme.for: A Bunsen burner
B inoculating loop
C culture bottle
D Petri dish

hints: B is the tool that carries the bacteria. Its name is examined on its own, so learn both words.
parts.workedSolution: A is the Bunsen burner, B the inoculating loop, C the culture bottle and D the Petri dish.

parts.stem: Explain why the transfer is carried out close to the Bunsen burner.

accepted: the rising hot air carries microorganisms up and away from the agar

scheme.for: rising (hot) air carries microorganisms away / reduces contamination from the air

hints: What does the air above a flame do?
parts.workedSolution: Hot air rising from the flame carries microorganisms up and away from the agar, which reduces contamination from the air.

context.setting: Sterilising apparatus and protecting a culture

parts.stem: An inoculating loop is sterilised by heating it until it glows red. Name the piece of apparatus that heats it.

scheme.for: Bunsen burner

hints: The loop is heated until it glows.
parts.workedSolution: A Bunsen burner: the loop is held in the flame until it glows red hot.

parts.stem: Before bacteria are cultured, some equipment is sterilised in an autoclave. Name two items that are sterilised this way.

scheme.for: any two from: Petri dishes / culture media (agar, nutrient broth) / culture bottles / inoculating loops
second, different item

hints: An autoclave is a pressure cooker for equipment: think of what the bacteria will touch.
parts.workedSolution: Petri dishes and culture bottles (culture media and inoculating loops can be sterilised this way too).

commonErrors.feedback: The Bunsen burner is what sterilises the loop; it never goes into the autoclave. The autoclave takes whatever will touch the culture: dishes, media, bottles.

parts.stem: While the agar is being inoculated, the Petri dish is opened only a crack. Explain why.

accepted: to stop microorganisms from the air landing on the agar and contaminating it

scheme.for: to reduce or stop contamination / microorganisms from the air entering the dish

hints: What is the lid protecting the agar from?
parts.workedSolution: To stop microorganisms from the air landing on the agar and contaminating the culture.

commonErrors.feedback: The danger runs the other way, and it is not the air itself: the lid stops microorganisms carried in the air from getting in and landing on the agar.

parts.stem: The incubator is set no higher than 25 °C. Explain why.

accepted: to avoid growing pathogens, the bacteria that cause disease in humans

scheme.for: to reduce or stop the growth of pathogens / harmful bacteria

hints: Which bacteria grow best at the temperature of a human body?
parts.workedSolution: To avoid growing pathogens: bacteria that cause disease in humans are adapted to body temperature, 37 °C, so keeping the dish at 25 °C or below makes it unlikely that any will grow.

commonErrors.feedback: The limit is not there to help the culture grow. It is a safety limit: bacteria that cause disease in humans grow best near body temperature, so staying at 25 °C or below avoids growing them.

parts.stem: Explain why the bench is wiped with disinfectant after the plates have been set up.

accepted: to kill any bacteria left on the bench

scheme.for: to kill / remove any bacteria (microorganisms) left on the bench

hints: Say what the disinfectant does to the bacteria, not only why bacteria are a problem.
parts.workedSolution: To kill any bacteria that were spilt or left on the bench, so nobody picks them up later.

commonErrors.feedback: That says why bacteria matter, not what the cleaning does. The mark is for the action: the disinfectant kills or removes any bacteria left on the bench.

context.setting: The order of the steps in an aseptic transfer

parts.stem: Put the steps for transferring bacteria from a culture bottle onto an agar plate in the correct order.

expectedOrder: Heat the inoculating loop in the Bunsen flame until it glows red hot
Let the loop cool for a few seconds
Remove the lid of the culture bottle and pass its neck through the flame
Dip the loop into the culture, then flame the neck again and replace the lid
Lift the Petri dish lid a little and streak the loop across the agar
Tape the lid on and incubate the dish at no more than 25 °C

scheme.for: loop heated until red hot and cooled before it touches the culture
bottle neck flamed and sample taken before the dish is opened; dish taped and incubated last

hints: The loop is sterilised first, and it must be cool before it touches anything alive.
parts.workedSolution: Heat the inoculating loop in the Bunsen flame until it glows red hot. Let the loop cool for a few seconds. Remove the lid of the culture bottle and pass its neck through the flame. Dip the loop into the culture, then flame the neck again and replace the lid. Lift the Petri dish lid a little and streak the loop across the agar. Tape the lid on and incubate the dish at no more than 25 °C.

pattern.regex: Dip the loop into the culture[^;\n]*Heat the inoculating loop

commonErrors.feedback: Heating the loop after it has picked up the bacteria kills the bacteria you meant to transfer. The loop is sterilised first, cooled, and only then dipped into the culture.

context.setting: Two agar plates after incubation, one of them contaminated

figures.alt: Two round dishes seen from above after incubation, side by side. Both show rows of small dots along zig-zag streak lines. The dish on the right also shows three large round growths with fringed edges and two smaller round growths with a dark centre, lying in the gaps between the rows of dots.

parts.stem: Two students each streaked the same bacterium onto an agar plate. The diagram shows the two plates side by side after incubation. Which plate has been contaminated?

options.feedback: The left-hand plate shows only one kind of colony, and every colony lies on a streak line: that is a pure culture.
The right-hand plate. Its large fringed growths and its ringed colonies are not the bacterium that was streaked.

scheme.for: the right-hand plate

parts.workedSolution: The plate on the right.

parts.stem: Give one piece of evidence from the diagram for your answer.

accepted: it has colonies of other kinds, away from the streak lines

scheme.for: colonies of a different type / shape / size, or colonies growing away from the streak lines

hints: Compare the colonies with the ones on the left-hand plate, and look at where they are.
parts.workedSolution: The right-hand plate has colonies of other kinds, larger and differently shaped, and they grow away from the streak lines, so they did not come from the loop.

parts.stem: Suggest one mistake in aseptic technique that could have caused this contamination.

accepted: the lid was lifted too far, so microorganisms from the air fell onto the agar

scheme.for: any valid lapse: lid lifted too far or left off / loop or bottle neck not flamed / not working near the Bunsen / bench not cleaned

hints: Think of each way a microorganism from the air, the bench or a hand could reach the agar.
parts.workedSolution: The lid was lifted too far or left off for too long, so microorganisms from the air landed on the agar (an unflamed loop or a dirty bench would also explain it).

context.setting: Finding the food that carried salmonella at a club barbecue

data.caption: Foods eaten at a club barbecue

parts.stem:
The table shows how many people at a club barbecue ate each food, and how many of them became ill with salmonella food poisoning the next day.
Calculate the percentage of the people who ate burgers who became ill. Give your answer to one decimal place.
hints: Divide by the people who ate burgers, not by everybody at the barbecue.

commonErrors.feedback: The fraction has been turned upside down: 80 ÷ 26 gives more than 100%, which cannot be a share of a group. The number who became ill goes on top: 26 ÷ 80 × 100.

parts.stem: Which food most likely carried the salmonella bacteria? Use percentages from the table to explain your answer.

accepted: burgers: 32.5% of the people who ate them became ill, the highest percentage, compared with 20.0% for coleslaw and 8.3% for ice cream

scheme.for: burgers
the highest percentage of those who ate it became ill (32.5%)
scheme.examinerNote: Comparative language is the mark: 'the highest percentage', not 'a high percentage'.

scheme.for: compares with the percentage for another food: coleslaw 20.0% or ice cream 8.3%

hints: Work out a percentage for every food first, then compare them with a word ending in -est.

parts.stem: Name the type of microorganism that causes salmonella food poisoning.

scheme.for: bacterium / bacteria

hints: It is one of the three bacterial diseases on the specification.
parts.workedSolution: A bacterium.

commonErrors.feedback: Salmonella is a bacterium, which is why antibiotics can treat it. The viral diseases on the specification are HIV, cold and flu, and HPV.

parts.stem: Give one way the organisers could have prevented this outbreak.

scheme.for: cook meat thoroughly / wash hands / keep raw and cooked food apart / keep food chilled

hints: Where do the bacteria come from, and what kills them?
parts.workedSolution: Cook the burgers thoroughly, all the way through, which kills the bacteria (washing hands and keeping raw meat away from cooked food also work).

Complete the table using words from this list. Each word is used once.
antibiotics     condom     fungicide     vaccination

scheme.for: chlamydia prevention: condom
chlamydia treatment: antibiotics
potato blight prevention: fungicide
flu prevention: vaccination

parts.stem: HIV leads to AIDS. Give one way HIV is spread.

scheme.for: sexual intercourse / sharing needles / blood / from mother to baby

hints: Two main routes: one sexual, one through blood.
parts.workedSolution: Through unprotected sex (or by sharing needles).

parts.stem: Give the term for the techniques used to grow microorganisms safely without contaminating them.

parts.stem: Give the maximum temperature at which bacterial cultures should be incubated in a school laboratory.
hints: Well below body temperature.

commonErrors.feedback: 37 °C is body temperature, the temperature pathogens grow best at, which is exactly what the limit exists to avoid. The maximum is 25 °C.

parts.stem:
A student is going to grow bacteria from a culture bottle on an agar plate. Describe the aseptic techniques she should use to transfer the bacteria to the plate, and to incubate the plate and dispose of it safely.
This question also assesses the quality of your written communication, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; everything set out in a clear and sensible order; spelling, punctuation and grammar make the meaning clear throughout.

Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; an order you can follow, though it is not held right through; spelling, punctuation and grammar are competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; ideas in an order that is hard to follow; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave what you meant unclear.

indicativeContent.point: heat the inoculating loop in the Bunsen flame until it glows red hot
let the loop cool before it touches the culture, or it kills the bacteria
take the lid off the culture bottle and pass the neck through the flame
dip the loop into the culture to pick up a loopful of bacteria
put the bottle lid back on straight away, never putting it down on the bench
keyWords: holding it rather than putting it on the bench

indicativeContent.point: work beside the Bunsen burner and lift the Petri dish lid only a little
streak the loop across the surface of the agar
close the lid, seal it with tape and label the dish
incubate at no more than 25 °C so that pathogens are not grown
autoclave the cultures before disposal, then clean the bench and wash hands

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: An answer that only sterilises the apparatus beforehand, and never moves any bacteria, stays in Band C: the question is about the transfer itself. For Band A, at least one point must be about the Petri dish.

hints: Follow the bacteria: loop, bottle, loop again, dish, incubator, autoclave. Every step has a safety reason.
The words that lift an answer are red hot, cool, neck, flame, lid only a little, streak, tape, 25 °C and autoclave.
parts.workedSolution: She heats the inoculating loop in the Bunsen flame until it glows red hot, then lets it cool for a few seconds so that it will not kill the bacteria. She takes the lid off the culture bottle, holding it rather than putting it on the bench, and passes the neck of the bottle through the flame. She dips the loop into the culture to pick up a loopful of bacteria, flames the neck again and puts the lid back on. Working beside the Bunsen burner, where rising air carries microorganisms away, she lifts the lid of the Petri dish only a little and streaks the loop across the surface of the agar. She closes the lid, seals it with tape and labels the dish, then incubates it at no more than 25 °C so that pathogens are not grown. Afterwards the cultures are killed in an autoclave before disposal, and she cleans the bench and washes her hands.

commonErrors.feedback: 37 °C is body temperature: the temperature at which pathogens thrive. The incubator is set to 25 °C at most.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ciara is asked: 'Describe how to grow a pure culture of bacteria safely on an agar plate. [4]'
Her plan, one line for each stage:
studentWorking: Sterilise: wipe the bench with disinfectant; heat the loop until red hot, then let it cool.
Transfer: lift the lid of the dish only a little and streak the bacteria across the agar.
Seal: tape the lid on the dish and label it.
Incubation temperature = 37 °C, so the bacteria grow as quickly as possible.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 4 sets the incubator to body temperature. 37 °C is where pathogens grow best, so the plan could grow a disease-causing bacterium by accident; the limit is 25 °C.
correction: Sterilise: wipe the bench with disinfectant; heat the loop until red hot, then let it cool.
Transfer: lift the lid of the dish only a little and streak the bacteria across the agar.
Seal: tape the lid on the dish and label it.
Incubation temperature = 25 °C at most, to avoid growing pathogens.
findTheMistake.feedback: Three of the four marks stand: sterilising, the careful transfer and sealing are all right. The last mark needs the right number and the right reason together. It is a safety limit, not a growth setting: 25 °C, to avoid growing pathogens.

prompts.prompt: Give two costs of disease to society.
